items.title: A block induced from a subgroup
items.statement: Fix a splitting p-modular system and write k for its residue field. For H≤G and a block b of kH, the induced block b^G is the unique block B of kG, when one exists, for which the (kH,kH)-bimodule b is an indecomposable direct summand of Res^{G×G}_{H×H} B. Block induction is undefined when there is no such unique B.
items.strategy: Regard block ideals as modules for the double groups. Krull–Schmidt makes the words 'direct summand' and 'unique block' unambiguous. Keep definedness explicit; no theorem on this page silently assigns b^G outside its stated hypotheses. Later compare this formulation with the central-character/Brauer-map criterion on the normalizer interval where that criterion is available.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Definition 5.13, p. 42
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Definition 40.1, p. 2

items.title: Induced blocks have controlled defect
items.statement: If b is a block of kH with defect group D and b^G is defined, then D is contained in a defect group of b^G (after the usual G-conjugation of the latter).
items.strategy: Choose ΔD as a vertex of the indecomposable k[H×H]-module b. Since b is a summand of Res B, Mackey vertex containment places ΔD in an (H×H)-conjugate of an intersection of H×H with a conjugate of a diagonal vertex ΔE of B. Projecting to G gives D≤_G E. This proves only containment, not equality.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Lemma 5.14(i), pp. 42–43
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Proposition 40.3(i), pp. 2–3

items.title: Centralizer containment makes block induction well-defined
items.statement: Let b be a block of kH with defect group D. If C_G(D)≤H≤G, then b^G is defined. If in addition H≤N_G(D), its block idempotent is equivalently selected by the traditional central-character formula λ_{b^G}=λ_b∘Br_D on class sums.
items.strategy: For existence, use that b is a summand of Res Ind_{ΔH}^{G×G}k and hence of the restriction of at least one block of kG. If two blocks contain b, a Mackey summand with vertex ΔD forces a double coset representative (x,y) with D≤H∩xHy^{-1}; the element x^{-1}y centralizes D, hence lies in H, so both summands occur in the same block. On H≤N_G(D), compute central characters on class sums localized by Br_D; multiplicativity and uniqueness of primitive central idempotents identify the same block. The Brauer-map clause is not asserted for arbitrary H.

references.title: Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Proposition 40.3(iii), pp. 3–4
Martínez, Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 4.5, pp. 24–25

items.title: Block induction is transitive when both stages are defined
items.statement: For K≤H≤G and a block c of kK, if c^H and (c^H)^G are defined, then c^G is defined and c^G=(c^H)^G. Equivalently, whenever the displayed induced blocks are defined, block induction composes transitively.
items.strategy: Restriction is transitive, so c is a summand of every global block containing c^H. Conversely, if c is a summand of a restricted global block B, uniqueness defining c^H makes c^H a summand of Res_H B; uniqueness defining (c^H)^G then forces B=(c^H)^G. This proves existence and equality together and never treats an undefined expression as a block.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Lemma 5.14(ii), p. 43
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Proposition 40.3(ii), p. 3

items.title: A global block of defect D determines a local block of defect D
items.statement: Assume AC. Fix a p-subgroup D≤G and N=N_G(D). If B is a block of kG having D as a defect group, then there is a block b of kN of defect group D such that b^G=B.
items.strategy: Choose a maximal B-Brauer pair (D,e) to fix the literal representative D rather than a canonical representative of its conjugacy class. Apply Green correspondence for G×G and ΔD to the block bimodule B. In the restriction of kG to N×N, the double-coset exclusion places every summand whose vertex contains ΔD inside the kN summand; hence the distinguished summand is itself an indecomposable block b of kN. Its vertex is exactly ΔD, so its defect group is D, and the summand relation gives b^G=B. AC is used only through the cited Green-correspondence theorem's selection of indecomposable summands; no stronger recorded set theory is used.

references.title: Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.4, pp. 4–5
Craven, The Brauer Correspondence, Theorem 1.12, pp. 9–10

items.title: Distinct local full-defect blocks induce to distinct global blocks
items.statement: Assume AC. Fix D≤G and N=N_G(D). If b and c are blocks of kN with defect group D and b^G=c^G, then b=c.
items.strategy: Both b and c have diagonal vertex ΔD. Under Green correspondence for G×G relative to ΔD, each is the unique distinguished N×N summand of the common induced/global block B=b^G=c^G. Uniqueness of that summand forces b≅c as bimodules, and distinct block ideals are nonisomorphic indecomposable summands of kN. AC occurs only in the cited Green-correspondence result.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Theorem 5.16, pp. 43–44
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.4, pp. 4–5

items.title: Every local full-defect block induces to a global block of defect D
items.statement: Assume AC. Fix D≤G and N=N_G(D). For every block b of kN with defect group D, block induction b^G is defined and b^G has defect group D.
items.strategy: Because C_G(D)≤N_G(D), centralizer containment first defines b^G. Green-correspond the indecomposable N×N-module b of vertex ΔD. The defining restriction summand and uniqueness in Green correspondence identify b^G with its distinguished G×G correspondent, whose vertex is exactly ΔD; hence b^G has defect group D. This also covers the possibility that the relevant block sets are empty. AC is used only through Green correspondence.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Theorem 5.16, pp. 43–44
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.4, pp. 4–5

items.title: Brauer's First Main Theorem
items.statement: Assume AC. Let D be a fixed p-subgroup of a finite group G and N=N_G(D). Block induction b↦b^G is a bijection from the blocks of kN having D as a defect group to the blocks of kG having D as a defect group. The assertion is a bijection of possibly empty sets and is equivariant under replacing D by a G-conjugate; it does not choose a canonical representative of a defect conjugacy class.
items.strategy: Surjectivity is the local-block existence lemma, well-definedness on every local full-defect block is the surjectivity lemma, and injectivity is separate. Check the D=1 and N=G boundaries explicitly: the same proof applies and the map is the identity when N=G. AC is inherited exactly from the three Green-correspondence lemmas.

references.title: Martínez, Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 4.10, pp. 27–28
Craven, The Brauer Correspondence, Theorem 1.12, pp. 9–10
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.4, pp. 4–5

items.title: The Brauer correspondent of a block
items.statement: Assume AC and fix an actual defect group D of a block B of kG. The Brauer correspondent of B in N_G(D) is the unique defect-D block b of kN_G(D) satisfying b^G=B. Replacing D by gDg^{-1} replaces b by its g-conjugate, so the construction is canonical only up to that conjugacy.
items.strategy: This definition is introduced only after the bijection: existence and uniqueness are precisely the surjective and injective halves of the First Main Theorem. Record D as data and never pretend that its conjugacy class has a preferred representative.

references.title: Martínez, Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 4.10, pp. 27–28
Craven, The Brauer Correspondence, Definition following Theorem 1.12, p. 10

items.title: Corresponding block bimodules are Green correspondents
items.statement: Assume AC. If B is a block of kG with defect group D and b is its Brauer correspondent in N=N_G(D), then the indecomposable block bimodules B and b are Green correspondents for G×G and N×N with respect to ΔD.
items.strategy: The proof of the bijection constructs b as the unique distinguished N×N summand in Res B with vertex ΔD. Conversely, induction of b has B as its unique distinguished G×G summand. These two uniqueness assertions are exactly the Green-correspondence characterization. AC is used through that theorem and nowhere else.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Theorem 5.16, pp. 43–44
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.4, pp. 4–5

items.title: Brauer–Green block compatibility
items.statement: Let Q≤G, let H≤G contain Q C_G(Q), and let V be an indecomposable kG-module with vertex Q. If U is an indecomposable direct summand of Res^G_H V with vertex Q, b is the block of kH containing U, and B is the block of kG containing V, then b^G is defined and equals B.
items.strategy: Centralizer containment first makes b^G defined. Let e be the central idempotent of B. If b^G≠B, then e annihilates the b-component predicted by induction. Split U into Res V and express the split map through eB⊗_k V. The block-bimodule Mackey decomposition and the double-coset exclusion force every relevant summand to be relatively projective for a proper subgroup of Q, contradicting that U has vertex Q. This is the complete direct block-idempotent proof; it does not consume the later Nagao decomposition theorem or AC.

references.title: Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.5, pp. 5–7
Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Theorem 5.17 and Corollary 5.18, pp. 44–45

items.title: Every block contains a module whose vertex is a full defect group
items.statement: Assume AC. If B is a block of kG with defect group D, then B contains an indecomposable kG-module whose vertex is D.
items.strategy: Let b be the Brauer correspondent in N=N_G(D). Since D is normal in N and is a defect group of b, p-radicality gives D=O_p(N). Choose a simple b-module S and take its indecomposable projective cover P over k[N/D]; inflation keeps P in b and makes it a summand of Ind_D^N k, hence relatively D-projective. Restricting back to D gives copies of the trivial kD-module, whose vertex is D, so vertex retention forces P itself to have vertex D. Its Green correspondent V has vertex D; block compatibility puts V in b^G=B. AC enters only through existence of the selected correspondent under the published Green theorem.

references.title: Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Corollary 40.7, pp. 7–8
Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Corollary 5.19, p. 45

items.title: Brauer correspondence for a defect-D8 block of S7 in characteristic 2
items.statement: Assume AC and let k have characteristic 2. In G=S7 take D=⟨(12),(1324)⟩≅D8 on {1,2,3,4}. Then N_G(D)=D×S3. The unique nonprincipal block of kN_G(D) with defect group D is the Brauer correspondent of the defect-D block of kS7; the principal local block has the larger Sylow defect D×C2.
items.strategy: Compute the normalizer from disjoint supports. Use the characteristic-2 block data tabulated in the source: kS7 has the indicated defect-D block, while k(D×S3) has a principal block of Sylow defect and one nonprincipal block of defect D. The First Main Theorem forces the latter pair. Do not use the source's later conjectural placement of individual ordinary characters. AC is inherited from the theorem.

references.title: Craven, The Brauer Correspondence, §1.6 example for S7, pp. 13–16

items.title: Brauer correspondence for SL2(Fp) in defining characteristic
items.statement: Assume AC, let p>2, G=SL2(F_p), let D be the lower-unitriangular Sylow p-subgroup, and N=N_G(D) the lower-triangular subgroup. The two positive-defect blocks of kG, containing respectively the odd-index and even-index simple modules in the standard list, correspond to the two defect-D blocks of kN detected by the matching parity of the heads of their Green correspondents; the Steinberg block is defect zero and is not in this defect-D bijection.
items.strategy: Use the explicit restriction of each standard simple G-module V_i to N: it is indecomposable with vertex D and head U_{i-1}, and its composition factors have fixed parity. This identifies its Green correspondent and hence its local block. Apply block compatibility and First Main to pair the two parity blocks, while separating the projective Steinberg module. AC is inherited from First Main/Green correspondence.

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Examples 4.31 and 5.5, pp. 37–39, 42

items.title: Centralizer containment is sufficient but not necessary
items.statement: Let p=2, let G=D_{2n} with n odd, and let H=C_n be its normal 2-complement. The principal block b_0(H) has trivial defect and b_0(H)^G=b_0(G) is defined, although C_G(1)=G is not contained in H. Thus C_G(D)≤H is not necessary for block induction to exist.
items.strategy: Since H has odd order, kH is semisimple and its principal block is the trivial module. Restricting the principal block bimodule of kG contains that block, and the normal-complement block calculation gives uniqueness, hence b_0(H)^G=b_0(G). But the relevant local defect group is 1, whose centralizer is all of G. The smallest instance n=3 is D6≅SL2(2).

references.title: Saunders, Modular Representation Theory, Example 5.15, p. 43

items.title: The trivial-defect-group and identity-normalizer boundaries
items.statement: Assume AC. For D=1 one has N_G(D)=G, and Brauer's First Main Theorem is the identity bijection on defect-zero blocks. More generally, whenever N_G(D)=G, its defect-D bijection is the identity. These assertions remain valid when the relevant sets of blocks are empty.
items.strategy: Substitute D=1 or N_G(D)=G into the definition of block induction: restriction from G×G to itself is the identity and every block is its own unique inducing block. Relate the case D=1 to numerical defect zero, and explicitly observe that the identity map on the empty set is a bijection. The inherited AC hypothesis is harmless here; the boundary calculation itself is choice-free.

references.title: Martínez, Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 4.10, pp. 27–28
Farrell–Lassueur, Modular Representation Theory of Finite Groups, Theorem 40.4, pp. 4–5
